nameStory: Sessile Dodder gets its name from its flowers that sit directly on the stem without stalks - 'sessile' means sitting or attached without a stem in botanical terms. The word 'dodder' comes from an old English term meaning to shake or tremble, referring to how these thread-like parasitic vines seem to quiver in the breeze as they wrap around their host plants.
description: Sessile Dodder is a parasitic vine that looks like tangled orange or yellow spaghetti wrapped around trees and shrubs. Unlike most plants, it has no leaves and doesn't make its own food through photosynthesis - instead, it attaches to woody plants and steals nutrients directly from them. The thin, thread-like stems can form dense mats that completely cover their host plants. This sneaky plant produces tiny white or cream-colored flowers clustered tightly along its stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Leafless, thread-like orange to yellow stems that spiral around woody plants like a living rope, forming tangled masses that can cover entire shrubs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or cream bell-shaped flowers clustered in tight, compact groups that sit directly on the stem without flower stalks, feeling slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, stringy stems about as thick as yarn that feel slightly sticky and break easily when pulled, ranging from bright orange to pale yellow

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Small, peg-like structures called haustoria that pierce into the host plant's stem like tiny vampiric fangs, visible as slight swellings where the dodder touches its host

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Completely absent - what look like tiny scales along the stem are actually reduced leaf remnants that serve no function

habitat: Found wrapped around woody shrubs and small trees in forest edges, thickets, and disturbed woodlands throughout New England, though quite rare with only a couple confirmed sightings in the region. Prefers areas with plenty of suitable host plants like dogwoods, elderberries, and other native shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Young dodder plants emerge from seed and begin seeking host plants, appearing as tiny orange threads reaching out from the soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the bright orange tangles are most visible, with tiny white flowers appearing in compact clusters along the stems from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Stems may persist and continue growing until first frost, with small round seed capsules developing after flowering.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely, surviving only as seeds in the soil that will germinate the following spring.

funFact: Sessile Dodder seeds can actually 'smell' their preferred host plants and will grow toward the chemical scents released by woody shrubs, essentially hunting for their victims before they even make contact!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dodder species, but Sessile Dodder specifically targets woody plants while most other dodders prefer herbaceous hosts like wildflowers and grasses. The compact, sessile flower clusters (sitting right on the stem) distinguish it from Field Dodder and Scaldweed, which have flowers on short stalks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being parasitic, dodders aren't necessarily 'bad' plants - they're native species that have evolved alongside their hosts for millions of years and rarely kill healthy plants. However, they can stress already weakened plants and may impact garden shrubs if they become established.
compareHints: Sessile Dodder is unique among New England dodders for specializing on woody hosts rather than soft-stemmed plants. Its flowers are more tightly clustered and sit directly on the stem, unlike Scaldweed and Field Dodder which have flowers on short stalks. The orange coloration tends to be more intense than most other dodder species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scaldweed differs from its dodder relatives primarily in where it grows - it prefers wetter habitats than Field Dodder, and its stems tend to be slightly thicker than Five Angled Dodder.
Compared to other dodders in New England, field dodder produces the largest seeds and tends to form denser, more tangled masses.

Buttonbush Dodder differs from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and host preferences - while Field Dodder attacks crops and Scaldweed Dodder prefers woodland edges, Buttonbush Dodder is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Lizard's tail dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and highly specific host preference for lizard's tail plants.
Smartweed Dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its habitat and host preferences - it's the wetland specialist of the dodder family.
Among New England's dodder species, hazel dodder is distinguished by its preference for woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants.
Five Angled Dodder is much rarer in New England than the common Scaldweed dodder, and prefers wetter habitats compared to Field Dodder's preference for dry agricultural areas.
